Conclusion The Committee has carefully examined the programme Based Budget Estimates for Parliament and the Parliamentary Service and found the programmes and policies planned for the 2025 Financial year to be necessary towards achieving the goals and objectives of the Parliament of Ghana. However, in light of the limited fiscal space, the Committee strongly recommends that the Ministry of Finance conducts a thorough review of Parliament's budget during its mid-year review. The Committee believes that a reassessment of the figures is necessary to ensure that Parliament is adequately funded to carry out its key functions, including the execution of proposed projects and statutory obligations. The Committee accordingly recommends to the House to adopt this report and approve the sum of one billion, one hundred and sixteen million, one hundred and ninety-nine thousand, five hundred and eleven Ghana Cedis (GH₵1,116,199,511.00) for the services of Parliament and the Parliamentary Service for the 2025 financial year. The Constitution provides in article 178(1)(a) that: “No moneys shall be withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund except — (a) to meet expenditure that is charged on that Fund by this Constitution or by an Act of Parliament;” The same term is used there: “charged”. Similarly, article 179 elaborates on the authorisation of 13 22nd December, 2023 14 Statements Government expenditure, including the preparation of Budget Estimates by the President, which are then laid before Parliament. By reading these provisions conjunctively, it becomes clear that article 108(a)(ii) is concerned with direct payments and explicit financial obligations from the Consolidated Fund and other public funds, primarily related to Government expenditure. These are not just incidental or indirect financial implications, but are specifically about the allocation and use of State funds in a direct manner. To further ground this analysis, Hon Members, let us consider chapter 13 of the 1992 Constitution which deals with finance. This chapter provides the necessary context for dealing with fiscal matters elaborating on the processes and principles governing the management of public funds, budgetary allocations, taxation, and financial legislation. Reading articles 108, 178, and 179 together, one can come to the conclusion that article 108(a)(ii) relates to direct payments and financial obligations from the Consolidated Fund and other public funds to meet Government’s expenditure. Now, let us consider the nature of the Bills in question. While they may carry financial implications, primarily related to the costs of incarceration and health care, these do not amount to the direct imposition of a new charge on the Consolidated Fund or other public funds. The financial implications here are consequential and incidental, rather than being the creation of a new fiscal obligation. Therefore, interpreting these Bills as falling within the ambits of fiscal legislation as outlined in article 108(a)(ii), stretches the meaning of “imposition of a charge” beyond its intended scope. Hon Members, it is imperative to underscore that literal and narrow interpretation of fiscal Bills could unduly constrict the legislative autonomy granted to Parliament. Such an approach would not only be contrary to the spirit of the Constitution, but would also set a precedent that could hinder our ability to address the diverse needs of our nation through Private Member’s legislation. Hon Members, the Bills under consideration do not create new fiscal obligations; therefore, should not be constrained by the provisions of article 108. It is worth noting that, neither the President nor Parliament has such power to declare an Act unconstitutional. Out of the abundance of caution, I must note that article 2(1) of the Constitution outlines that any allocation of any unconstitutionality must of necessity be grounded in the course of action before the Supreme Court. The Constitution vests the power to declare an Act unconstitutional solely in the Supreme Court. This principle is central to the doctrine of separation of powers and the rule of law. Mr Speaker, there was another concern that if one looks at the allocation made for the various Committees as against the expenditure on foreign travels, people were concerned that we have to ensure that these allocations are boosted to take care of the local activities that are undertaken in the country to ensure that we are able to pursue our oversight responsibility responsibly. Mr Speaker: Hon Members, before I put the question, please, it does not lie in the mouth of Parliament to always complain that the budget allocation to Parliament is on the low side. This is because you approve it; you are the people who decide how much should be given to you. So, who are you complaining to? Who should increase your budget for you? You are the same people who decide, for whatever reason, to give yourself a low budget. Then after that, you are demanding that those administering the budget let you do other things that are not captured in the budget. That is not possible. We have tried for some time now to always find something for the former Members of Parliament and the former staff of Parliamentary Service, and we have allowed them the free use of the Parliament Medical Centre.
